strengths: The paper addresses a significant and practical problem in trustworthy machine learning: mitigating spurious correlations and achieving group robustness without requiring explicit bias annotations during training or validation.

The empirical results are strong across both standard real-world benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments) and multi-class synthetic datasets (cMNIST, cCIFAR10 with varying bias conflict ratios), matching or outperforming several existing bias-agnostic and bias-supervised methods.
The proposed approach is computationally lightweight, avoiding complex bilevel optimizations, adversarial training, or expensive sample-level kernel density estimates required by original CCDB.
Ablation studies nicely decouple the contributions of BEO (as a proxy annotation tool integrated into GroupDRO and DFR) and FG-CCDB (evaluated with ground-truth annotations).
weaknesses: The setting assumes $|S| = |Y| = C$, which limits the applicability of the method when the cardinality of bias attributes does not match the number of target classes, or when multiple heterogeneous bias attributes exist simultaneously.

The motivation and formulation of Equations (3) and (4) warrant deeper justification against standard group-balanced weighting. Expanding $W_{i,j}$ yields $w_{i,j} \propto  rac{N_{i,\cdot} N_{\cdot,j}}{N \cdot N_{i,j}^2}$. It remains theoretically and empirically unclear why this specific weighting outperforms standard uniform group weighting ($w_{i,j} \propto 1/N_{i,j}$), and a baseline comparison against standard group-balanced sampling with BEO pseudo-labels is missing.

The bias exploration mechanism (BEO) relies on several empirical heuristics (e.g., training on a 10% random subset, selecting the top 50% most confident samples per class, repeating ERM training), which are closely related to prior sample-selection and agreement/disagreement schemes (such as SELF, JTT, and DPR) without a comprehensive comparative ablation of these design choices.

The manuscript contains several noticeable typos and grammatical errors that should be polished (e.g., 'foucus' on page 4, 'Rnadom Split' in Figure 1, 'finial' on page 7, 'muti-class' and 'bia-supervised' on page 9, 'BOE' vs 'BEO' inconsistent naming in Table 3).

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and practical problem: mitigating spurious correlations and improving group robustness without access to bias annotations during training or validation.
The overall pipeline is lightweight and avoids iterative or computationally intensive distribution optimization during the mitigation phase, relying on closed-form sample reweighting.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across both standard real-world benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments) and multi-class synthetic datasets (cMNIST, cCIFAR-10), showing competitive or superior worst-group accuracy compared to several bias-agnostic baselines.

Extensive ablations evaluate the bias exploration module (BEO) as a plug-in pseudo-labeler for existing methods like GroupDRO and DFR, providing insight into the quality of the learned bias groupings.
weaknesses: A major limitation of the approach is the rigid assumption that $|\mathcal{S}| = |\mathcal{Y}| = C$. Spurious attributes in real-world scenarios frequently do not match the cardinality of the label space (e.g., binary demographic/background attributes in multi-class problems, continuous nuisance attributes, or multiple concurrent biases). This severely restricts the applicability of BEO and FG-CCDB.

The theoretical justification for the reweighting formulation in Equations (2)–(4) is somewhat ad-hoc. Aligning each class-conditional distribution $P_{:,j}$ to the empirical marginal $q$ leaves the marginal distribution over bias attributes uncorrected and potentially heavily skewed. It is unclear why this objective is preferred over standard uniform group balancing (where $p(s, y)$ is set to uniform).

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: using overfitted or early-trained ERM models to separate bias-aligned and bias-conflicting instances is a well-explored concept in prior work (e.g., JTT, LfF, SELF, DPR). The primary variation here is selecting top-confidence samples to amplify bias, which is closely related to existing bias-amplification strategies.

There are several noticeable typos and presentation issues throughout the manuscript (e.g., 'Rnadom Split' in Figure 1, 'In the present of spurious correlations', 'which is rarely holds', 'base on CCDB', and 'finial unbiased learning' in Section 4).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: mitigating spurious correlations without requiring ground-truth bias annotations during either training or validation.

The proposed method provides a closed-form group reweighting formula (FG-CCDB) that avoids iterative min-max optimization or computationally expensive sample-wise feature covariance matching during the debiasing stage.

Competitive empirical results across standard group-robustness benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR-10), demonstrating substantial gains over prior bias-agnostic baselines such as CCDB, uLA, and ERM.
Ablation studies nicely decouple the effect of the bias discovery module (BEO) from the distribution balancing formulation (FG-CCDB).
weaknesses: Restrictive assumption on bias space cardinality (|S| = |Y|): The method fundamentally assumes that the number of bias attributes equals the number of target classes and that each class is spuriously correlated with exactly one corresponding bias attribute in a 1-to-1 fashion. This assumption holds in synthetic setups like cMNIST/cCIFAR-10 and binary benchmarks, but breaks down in realistic multi-class settings where biases are shared across multiple classes (e.g., common background textures shared across many animal categories) or where bias cardinality is arbitrary.

Close equivalence to error-split methods in the binary setting: When |Y| = 2, the BEO grouping matrix N simply partitions data into correctly classified (diagonal) and misclassified (off-diagonal) sets by the biased model f_{\theta_2}. This is structurally identical to error-split identification in JTT and SELF. The manuscript does not sufficiently discuss or analyze this direct connection.

Missing ablation against standard group-balanced weighting: Once pseudo-groups (s, y) are obtained via BEO, standard group balancing would assign each sample a weight proportional to 1 / N_{s,y}. FG-CCDB instead assigns weight W_{i,j} / N_{i,j} = q_i / (P_{i,j} N_{i,j}). The paper does not evaluate whether the specific distribution-matching weight formula provides any empirical benefit over standard inverse group-frequency weighting on the same discovered groups.

Model selection clarity: The paper states that model selection is performed using 'worst-class accuracy on the validation set' to remain bias-agnostic. However, on datasets where class distributions are balanced (e.g., Waterbirds), worst-class accuracy does not necessarily track worst-group accuracy. Further empirical verification and clarification on how sensitive this selection criterion is across benchmarks are needed.

Writing and proofreading errors: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting errors, including 'Rnadom Split' in Figure 1, 'banchmark' (p. 7), 'finial' (p. 7), 'To asses' (p. 9), 'bia-supervised' (p. 9), 'muti-class' (p. 9), and inconsistent naming ('BOE' vs. 'BEO' in Section 4.4 and Table 3).

strengths: Clear motivation: The paper targets a known limitation of Class-Conditional Distribution Balancing (CCDB)—the assumption of a single Gaussian distribution over bias features—and addresses it via discrete mode modeling derived from model confusion matrices.

Simplicity and computational efficiency: Mode-wise distribution matching yields closed-form sample weights (Equations 3 and 4), eliminating the need for iterative optimization or feature caching across the dataset during debiasing.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across standard single-shortcut datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut datasets (UrbanCars), and multi-class synthetic benchmarks (cMNIST, cCIFAR10), achieving competitive or superior worst-group accuracy (WGA) compared to leading bias-agnostic baselines and even supervised upper bounds on CivilComments.

Thorough ablation and diagnosis: The paper provides meaningful ablations separating the contribution of MST (tested with GroupDRO and DFR) and FG-CCDB (tested with ground-truth annotations), along with parameter sensitivity analysis on $\gamma$ and $\beta$.
weaknesses: Structural restriction $|S| = |Y|$: The bias label space is constrained to match the class label space because $s$ is defined by the auxiliary model's class predictions. In multi-shortcut or asymmetric bias settings (e.g., binary target with multiple distinct shortcut attributes, or multi-class target with binary bias), forcing the confusion matrix to be $C \times C$ collapses distinct underlying bias groups into a single mode.

Heuristic nature of high-confidence filtering: Filtering the top $\beta = 50\%$ samples per class relies heavily on the assumption that majority/bias-aligned samples dominate (>50%) and are learned faster. As the authors acknowledge in the conclusion, when bias proportions deviate (e.g., in datasets like CelebA or skewed multi-class setups), this heuristic can misidentify or dilute bias cues.

Incremental theoretical advance over CCDB: The mutual information debiasing framework (Equation 1) is adopted directly from Zhao et al. (2025). Discretizing the latent space via the confusion matrix effectively reduces CCDB to standard importance weighting over discrete groups, which, while pragmatic and effective, represents an incremental conceptual jump.

Unpolished appendix presentation: Appendix E is presented in a raw rebuttal format (headings such as 'R1W1', 'R1Q1', 'R2W1', 'R3Q1'), reflecting pasted responses from a previous submission rather than seamlessly integrated appendix text.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: learning group-robust representations under spurious correlations without requiring expensive human bias annotations.

The proposed FG-CCDB simplifies and improves upon the continuous Gaussian approximation in CCDB by deriving closed-form, mode-level sample weights directly from the confusion matrix, avoiding iterative weight optimization and feature storage overhead.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning standard binary benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), a multi-shortcut benchmark (UrbanCars), and extreme multi-class synthetic datasets (cMNIST, cCIFAR10). FG-CCDB consistently matches or outperforms strong bias-agnostic and several bias-supervised baselines.
The bias exploration quality of MST is thoroughly analyzed, including precision, recall, and F1 metrics for identifying minority modes across various iteration counts and sample selection fractions.
weaknesses: The framework intrinsically ties the spurious attribute label space to the target label space (|S| = |Y| = C) via the hard confusion matrix. In real-world scenarios, spurious attributes may not naturally correspond in cardinality to the target classes (e.g., binary target classification with multiple distinct background types, or fine-grained classes with binary spurious attributes).

The effectiveness of MST relies heavily on the 'simplicity bias' heuristic that ERM models overfit to spurious features first on small data subsets. As noted by the authors in the conclusion, this assumption can falter in cases with asymmetric bias distributions (such as CelebA or CivilComments) or when spurious attributes are not significantly easier to learn than core features.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental over CCDB and existing bias amplification literature (e.g., Lee et al., 2023; Ciranni et al., 2025). The closed-form weights in Equations (3) and (4) essentially correspond to an inverse-frequency style reweighting based on empirical joint counts of predicted vs. true labels.

Appendix E consists largely of unedited rebuttal responses from a previous submission cycle (labeled with reviewer identifiers such as R1W1, R2W2, R3Q1), which detracts from the professional formatting and self-contained structure of the manuscript.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in trustworthy machine learning: mitigating spurious correlations and achieving group robustness without requiring explicit bias annotations.

The proposed closed-form mode reweighting in FG-CCDB avoids the heavy optimization and full-dataset representation storage required by the continuous Gaussian approximation in CCDB, making sample reweighting simple and scalable.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide range of standard benchmarks, including real-world binary datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments), multi-shortcut settings (UrbanCars), and multi-class synthetic datasets (cMNIST, cCIFAR10).
Good ablation studies evaluating the quality of pseudo-group identification via MST (F1, precision, recall) and examining hyperparameter sensitivity (gamma, beta, and iteration counts).
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is relatively limited. The bias amplification via data selection (MST) largely mirrors existing observations that training on smaller subsets or high-confidence samples amplifies ERM simplicity bias (e.g., in JTT, Lee et al., Ciranni et al.). Furthermore, once the discrete mode matrix is constructed, the FG-CCDB reweighting in Equations (3) and (4) reduces to standard discrete importance weighting / marginal matching across confusion cells.

Rigid structural constraint on the bias space: MST assumes the bias label space has identical cardinality to the target classes (|S| = |Y| = C) simply by using the predictions of an overfitted C-class ERM model. In real-world multi-class datasets, spurious attributes often do not match the number of classes (e.g., binary background bias in a 10-class setting, or multiple continuous confounding factors), which limits the theoretical grounding and flexibility of equating the confusion matrix directly to the true bias modes.

Modest performance improvements on standard real-world datasets: On Waterbirds, CelebA, and CivilComments, the gains of FG-CCDB over strong existing bias-agnostic or pseudo-supervised baselines (such as CCDB, XRM, and SELF) are marginal or within error margins, with the primary significant improvements observed only on synthetic benchmarks (cMNIST and cCIFAR10).

Unpolished presentation in the supplementary material: Appendix E consists almost entirely of copied text from a previous review/rebuttal cycle (labeled with reviewer question headers such as 'R1W1', 'R1Q1', 'R2W1', etc.), which should have been integrated cleanly into the formal appendix text.
